newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs attack Commission review of waste policy.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs attack Commission review of waste policy.

text.p: The European Parliament continued an attacking spree over European Commission plans for new European Union environment laws on Thursday with a stinging condemnation of the Commission's review of EU waste policy.

It was the latest assault in a week in which the parliament slammed the Commission's plans to update the 1992-2000 EU environment action plan and EU law on environmental impact studies, and Green Euro-MPs called for Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard to resign.

Parliament passed a resolution on Thursday, drafted by Danish Socialist Kirsten Jensen, which said the Commission review of the EU's waste managment strategy -- COM(96)399 -- contained no forward-looking proposals and therefore failed to improve on the existing waste policy.
Euro-MPs demanded a new waste strategy by 1997, even though Bjerregaard had told them on Tuesday the Commission had no intention of drafting one.
They then attacked the review on a whole range of counts and asked the Commission to propose a long list of new environmental laws.

They said the review confused the notions of waste as an environmental problem and waste as a marketable product, and was unclear about the extent to which local and regional authorities should be responsible for waste planning.

The Commission talked about making producers liable for clearing up their waste but failed to say what "liability" meant or how a producer should be defined, taking into account that raw materials may undergo several processes before final use.
Neither did it propose chasing up member states which have largely failed to draft waste management plans, even though they are bound to do so by an EU law passed as long ago as 1975.

Continuing their criticisms, Euro-MPs poured scorn on the document's pledge to encourage taxes on virgin raw materials as a means of discouraging waste when the Commission had no proposals along these lines and was causing problems for national tax schemes by classifying them as barriers to trade.
The Commission spoke in favour of voluntary agreements to limit and manage waste properly, while its own document said existing accords on recycling paper were not respected.
It referred to the need to set new higher targets for the amount of waste which is sorted at source but did not specify what these targets should be, Euro-MPs complained.
The parliament took some comfort from the Commission's concern about violations of EU waste laws but was surprised that the Commission did not spell out what it intended to do.

Euro-MPs asked the Commission to hurry up and finalise its proposals on landfill sites; marking of packaging; acqueous discharge from hazardous waste; used tyres; end-of-life vehicles; health care waste; electrical and electronic waste; construction and demolition waste and hazardous domestic waste.

And they demanded new proposals for legislation on environmental liablility; taxes on virgin raw materials; levies on packaging, chlorinated solvents and heavy metals; targets for cutting waste volume and increasing recycling; environmental liability; and priority waste streams (rather than voluntary agreements).
